newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN UNIONS SEE DISASTER IN CAMDESSUS VISIT.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN UNIONS SEE DISASTER IN CAMDESSUS VISIT.

text.p: Powerful South African unions allied to President Nelson Mandela attacked a visit by IMF managing director Michel Camdessus on Friday, saying the Fund's policies courted disaster.

The International Monetary Fund leader, meeting Mandela earlier, gave his full backing to the government's macroeconomic plan to which the Congress of South African Trade Unions, Cosatu, refuses to give its full support.
"The IMF is not a friend of the working people or the majority of the South African people," COSATU deputy General Secretary Zwelinzima Vavi told a news conference.
"All their recommendations and policies have caused disasters in many developing countries in Africa."
Leaders of Cosatu, which is linked to Mandela's African National Congress and the South African Communist Party in a formal three-way alliance, refused to meet Camdessus.
They called for more transparency from the IMF and demanded that the government involve the union federation in negotiations with the Washington-based Fund.
"We want to be consulted on an approach so as to avoid falling into the same trap as other countries," Vavi said.

Protestors from non-governmental groups and unions lined up outside parliament in Cape Town, where Camdessus was to meet Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, to urge the government to reject stringent terms attached to IMF loans.
Protesters slammed the IMF's past record in Africa carrying placards saying "IMF, How many jobs have you axed today", and "IMF, Enemy of the poor".

Cosatu's Vavi said Camdessus's visit could derail talks between labour and government on implementing the marcoeconomic strategy, designed to boost annual economic growth to six percent by 2000 and slash unemployment.
"South Africa is in a very difficult process of developing national policies. The IMF's visit can only complicate these delicate negotiations between the role players," he said.

He accused the IMF of being two-faced by pledging to help South Africa control its budget deficit while refusing to write off a billion rand ($219 million) loan COSATU said had been given to the apartheid government in the 1980s.
"If they (IMF) are genuine in their commitment to the eradication of a budget deficit then this gentleman from Washington should write off this apartheid debt.
"We don't dispute the need for loans to be given to South Africa, but the IMF has a particular history of throwing countries into the deep end, with increased unemployment," Vavi said.
The ANC-led government has faced a fiery war of words and threats of crippling strikes from the 1.8-million member Cosatu over its plans to resuscitate the economy.

When the marcoeconomic strategy was unveiled in June, COSATU said its aims, such as lifting existing foreign exchange controls, undermined South Africa's reconstruction and development plans and could see millions lose work.
Camdessus is touring with IMF members in Southern Africa.
